items.title: Show HN: Flide: Make Jev-like decision models up to 9.5x faster
items.summary: Decision models need their own inference engine. So we developed Flide, a high-performance and exact inference engine for Jev-like decision models. Flide achieves up to a 9.5x speedup over vLLM and SGLang. It now supports 30+ popular local Jev-like decision models. Start to make your decision immediately: pip install flide Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50421155 Points: 25 # Comments: 4
items.content:
Flide is fast inference infrastructure for Jev-style decision models. With exact state forking it is up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang, and every answer is the one the model gives the question alone. It serves the Jev /v1/systemone API.

See the docs for every model, images, the API and all options.

Any model in the model table starts the same way, for example Perplexity's decision model.

The last three columns say how much faster Flide answers one request than the engine its release ships, as the median latency over the requests of each workload on one H200, where DI is the Decision Index. The chat models run against the faster of vLLM and SGLang, and OneJev against qev, the engine it used before Flide. KnowLine 35B runs with --quantize fp8 , as its release serves it in FP8. A value marked ~ is the average over the sizes tested.

Apache-2.0. flide/kernels/gdn.py holds a kernel derived from two kernels of flash-linear-attention (MIT); THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES lists it with the other code Flide builds on.

items.title: I libri scelti da Internazionale
items.summary: Da “Non correte! Andate piano!” di Roman Polanski a Grazie di Pablo Katchadjian. Le recensioni della stampa straniera Leggi
items.content:
Il regista Roman Polanski aveva già raccontato la sua infanzia durante la guerra in un’autobiografia: il muro che nel 1941 vede sorgere intorno al ghetto di Cracovia, i genitori deportati, la madre morta ad Auschwitz, il rifugio presso contadini polacchi. In “Non correte! Andate piano!” torna su quel passato. Per quanto gravi siano i fatti di violenza sessuale per i quali ha riportato condanne o è stato accusato, sarebbe un peccato non leggere il Polanski bambino rinchiuso nel ghetto. Il volume nasce da un’intervista del 2006 per l’Istituto nazionale dell’audiovisivo francese e la fondazione per la memoria della Shoah. Il rigore e l’interrogarsi continuo, accogliendo lacune e incomprensioni dei ricordi, trasformano la testimonianza orale in un ammirevole lavoro di scrittura. Il titolo riprende l’esortazione del lavoratore polacco che lo aiutò a uscire durante il rastrellamento che portò allo sgombero del ghetto, nel marzo 1943. Alle sue parole rispondono due testi del padre Ryszard: una lettera del 1973 sul percorso verso Maut-hausen e un secondo resoconto, datato 1976, sul campo di Płaszów. È una testimonianza agghiacciante e d’immenso coraggio. Il figlio cercava il padre; il padre, scampato più volte alla morte, sopravviveva per ritrovare il figlio. “L’inferno è vuoto, tutti i diavoli sono qui”, cita Polanski dalla Tempesta di Shakespeare, con un’eco del presente. Non è una profezia, ma una constatazione. Samuel Blumenfeld, Le Monde

Alla nuova narrativa argentina, rappresentata da Selva Almada, Federico Falco, Hernán Ronsino e Mauro Libertella, va aggiunto Pablo Katchadjian, che con Grazie dribbla gli avversari. Come il film Gangs of New York e il romanzo Middlesex di Eugenides, il romanzo comincia in un porto. Arrivano schiavi che padroni senza scrupoli selezionano e comprano. Uno di loro, senza nome, è costretto a lavori degradanti. L’umiliazione è tale che le mansioni non vengono descritte: conosciamo solo le reazioni del corpo. Per Walter Benjamin, i reduci tornavano dalla guerra in silenzio perché il trauma li aveva privati dell’esperienza. Così lo schiavo non trova parole per l’orrore: la violenza lo riduce a una cosa. Poi compaiono una bambina selvaggia, fiori dalle radici allucinogene e una serva oppressa. Nascono progetti di rivolta: non un’ideologia, ma il desiderio di un’emancipazione totale. Ucciso il padrone, il protagonista e i compagni partono per liberare altri schiavi, in auto, poi a piedi, incalzati da colonne di fumo. Definirlo solo un romanzo d’avventura sarebbe riduttivo: qui convivono sogno, allucinazione e politica non convenzionale. Non sappiamo dove né quando si svolga. La schiavitù è mutata, non abolita: la società dei consumi maschera lo sfruttamento. Il lavoro interinale non è forse un’evoluzione delle antiche sopraffazioni? Dinamico, divertente e imprevedibile, è all’opposto di quel che ci si aspetta. Katchadjian ha un’immaginazione smisurata. Joaquín Escobar, Ojo en tinta

Con Le forze , il suo secondo romanzo, la poeta Laura Vazquez propone un libro potente, che rischia di dividere per la forma e la radicalità del discorso. Odissea iniziatica, allucinata e caotica, romanzo-poema destabilizzante, Le forze è un’immersione per tappe nelle profondità dell’animo umano. Attraverso alcuni incontri, esplora contraddizioni, paradossi, alienazioni, fughe in avanti e superficialità, invitandoci a una vasta critica del mondo contemporaneo. La narratrice, una giovane donna che racconta di essere sopravvissuta all’infanzia, si domanda come vivere in un mondo schiacciato dal conformismo, dal denaro, dalla tirannia degli schermi e dalle parole d’ordine del capitalismo, la “grande forza” che nutriamo ogni giorno. Crescendo, ha osservato la sottomissione all’opinione comune, l’adesione passiva agli slogan, la ripetizione dei pregiudizi e il chiacchiericcio vuoto. Il dolore si è accumulato dentro di lei, formando mucchi, piramidi o cristalli. Da tempo porta con sé un’unica, vertiginosa certezza: “Il mondo mente”. Ritrovare la verità sotto le parole, forse perfino farla esistere, è un percorso che dipende dalla poesia, esperienza di osservazione e di linguaggio. Ma “il potere del suono è più grande di quello del senso”. Christian Desmeules, Le Devoir

Questa raccolta è molto meno spensierata di quanto il titolo possa far pensare: avere un debole per i cowboy può sembrare come una passione per il gelato, ma il bisogno ossessivo di partner incapaci di rispettarti non ha nulla di divertente. Con eroine che si stancano presto degli uomini addomesticati, Pam Houston può sembrare complice del maschio da divano, convinto di perdere il suo fascino primordiale se lava i piatti. Ma le sue protagoniste più originali sono troppo estreme per un maschilismo pigro. Alcol e linguaggio volgare sono giudicati più severamente nelle donne che negli uomini. Ma una così dovrebbe fingersi una pastorella di porcellana? Alcuni racconti, ironici e dolenti, sono poco realistici nella loro fiducia nel cambiamento: sembra basti del buon sesso con un uomo gentile per sistemare il mondo. La natura promette una cura, ma è troppo inospitale per ricavare facili lezioni morali. Altrove colpisce quanto le donne siano disposte a pagare pur di ricevere meno del dovuto. Houston sembra comprendere tutto delle situazioni che descrive, tranne il proprio bisogno di farne parte. Adam Mars-Jones, The Independent

items.title: A Critique of GPUI
items.summary: Article URL: https://blog.zortax.de/posts/a-critique-of-gpui Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50420857 Points: 95 # Comments: 55
items.content:
Recently, there has been a trend of more desktop GUI apps being built using native rust GUI frameworks. And there are now even well known electron apps getting official rewrites: Discord announced their app is being rewritten using GPUI. 1 Meanwhile, a lot of the LLM-clones being published seem to choose egui. In this post, I want to explain why I am not sure those frameworks are a good foundation to build on.

To put it plainly: I believe both GPUI’s and egui’s state models are dead ends for complex desktop applications. Both are impressive projects, and they have their place. Zed genuinely feels fast and nice to use, and I use egui myself for debug interfaces in bevy games. But I don’t think those frameworks should be the default choice for native desktop apps.

Disclosure: I ported GPUI’s current Linux renderer to wgpu 2 , I built the benchmark harness used below, and I work on zgui , a signal-based Rust framework that appears in the charts.

Raph Levien quotes Ron Minsky: “hidden inside of every UI framework is some kind of incrementalization framework.” 3 A UI is a function of state, and state changes a little at a time. But if that function becomes expensive, you might want to start looking for ways to derive a faster way to update pixels on the screen from an incremental state change. So every framework has to answer one question: when one value changes, what runs?

I understand why people like the first three. No state to synchronize, one place where state lives, a render function that is plain Rust, no macros or separate compiler. I’m gonna make the argument that these approaches don’t scale, and fixing the underlying problem defeats what makes these models simple and easy to reason about.

GPUI calls itself “a hybrid immediate and retained mode” framework. 4 It retains state in entities. The UI is defined in render functions, changing state must trigger a rerun.

It is ordinary Rust. You can use if , for and local variables, and there aren’t any weird wrappers. State changes require an explicit notification:

notify carries the entity id. 5 Since Rust doesn’t have a write barrier on &mut , GPUI cannot see which field changed (or whether anything changed at all). The Angular team wrote this about zone.js in 2023: it “is only capable of notifying us when something might have happened”, and “This approach has not scaled well.” 6 notify is more precise than a zone, since it names an entity, but ultimately it makes the same kind of statement. Below that id, GPUI knows nothing, so it re-renders every view that is not behind a valid .cached() boundary. And in practice, GPUI often rerender every view, because .cached() is rarely used by application authors, and imposes certain restrictions on layout semantics.

GPUI has a reputation of being “fast”. And while constants might be relatively low, asymptotically, it is leaving a lot on the table. So I ran a few benchmarks, that specifically test how much a sparse state change in a large UI actually costs.

At 3,000 live rows with a cached view per row, changing one label takes 8.4 ms. A hover, a keystroke and writing a value equal to the old one all cost about the same, because the cost follows the tree and not the change. It grows by about 3 ms per 1,000 live rows. Write the rows as plain elements, as in the code above, and the same label takes 92 ms. A hand-written equality guard takes the equal write from 7.9 ms to 0.9 µs (demonstrating how much is left for each call site to find).

This doesn’t mean that every GPUI app is slow, but it shows the limit of the state model. Especially with more expensive layout, you do hit this wall in practice. Zed might feel fast, but the truth is that Zed is a relatively simple app, UI wise. The app’s chrome contains a few buttons, in a simple layout, a sidebar and a text editor, and the text editor is implemented as a custom element, completely bypassing GPUI’s layout and view semantics. By their own account, a window “has tens of nodes and a few thousand elements”. 7

The obvious fix is to retain more. Zed has experimental branches for this, and Longbridge’s gpui-fast is a fork that keeps every view’s subtree between frames. 8 9 It works, within a limit: the smallest thing either one can reuse is a view. So to update one label without rebuilding the sidebar, the label has to be a view:

That is an entity, a Render impl, a subscription, a stored copy of the value, a hand-written guard and an owner, all to express that one label depends on one count. In a signal framework it is this:

The rest of GPUI’s API works against this too. Render takes no props, so parents push values into child entities during their own render. RenderOnce components, which is what buttons and rows are, draw inside their parent’s view and are no boundary at all. List rows are closures, so a row view means managing a keyed map of entities by hand.

And it only helps where state happens to line up with views. I reran gpui-fast’s own 60-panel benchmark, drew each frame once, and then moved the state:

With state owned by each panel, one change saves 83%. With a shared model, retention makes the same frame 11% slower. The window and the edit are identical. In real Zed, the Zed team measured retention “1–3% slower than off on ordinary workloads”, found that “Most of the real-Zed win” came from other work, and warned that “microbenchmark wins didn’t predict real-Zed results”. 8 gpui-fast is real progress and costs little to adopt: it takes the 3,000-row label from 8.4 to 3.4 ms. But that frame renders three views and lays out one element, and still spends 3.4 ms, because the frame is still a walk over the whole tree.

The web has already walked this road. Redux’s style guide says “Prefer having more UI components subscribed to the Redux store and reading data at a more granular level”. 10 MobX says to “create lots of small observer components”. 11 Both tell you to make a boundary per projection, manually, because the framework can’t infer it.

This is the part I find hardest to get past. People choose GPUI because render is a plain function of state. A UI where each projection is a separately owned entity with a subscription and a guard is no longer that. It is a signal graph built by hand from much heavier parts, where a missed edge is silent. Zed’s own design note says “Missing notifications are application bugs”. 12 Keep the pleasant API and you get view-sized updates. Take the precision and you lose the pleasant API. A signals crate on top would not change the trade, because its smallest sink is still a view. Reaching one node with no render running needs writes the framework can see and nodes that outlive a frame, and that means a new state model and a new element contract.

At the size it is usually shown, the Elm architecture is a deceptively simple UI model: one state value, one update , one view , and every change has a name. While large applications do use it successully, 13 14 I do want to make the point that this clarity belongs to the small case, and in a complex application signals and stores are arguably easier to reason about.

Take the same unread count. It has to be right after every message, so either view recomputes it on every update or update maintains it:

The definition of unread is now nowhere in particular. It is spread across every arm that touches a thread, and each new message has to remember it. The compiler checks that the match is exhaustive, but it does not check the arithmetic. The memo above has one definition, and a new writer cannot forget it.

The same thing happens with location. Where does a hover state or a half-typed draft live? Single source of truth says in the model, with a message type routed down and an outcome routed back up. Elm’s guide: “Actively trying to make components is a recipe for disaster in Elm.” 15 . Iced recommends returning an Action to the parent. 16 Iced’s maintainer says components in this architecture always end “with pain”, and also makes the best case for the discipline: avoiding them “forces you to think hard about your data model”. 17 Okay, I guess that’s a fair argument. But cosmic-files has 136 top-level message variants and 73 more for a tab, plus a Tab::update that returns commands for the parent to interpret. 18 Everything in that is explicit, and none of it is simple.

The architecture also has the same issue GPUI has. The update implementation tells you what a message writes, it cannot tell you what read the field. Anything inside the view might. Elm’s architecture doesn’t answer “what changed?”, it answers “what happened?”. Session export might be useful in some scenarios, but it is not useful for scalable performance characteristics. 19

This is what I read in the web’s history. Redux is the best-known relative of this design, and its docs read like a field report. Treat a portion of your store “as if it were a database”. 20 Selectors “will be re-run after every dispatched action”. 21 The core package is “obsolete”, replaced by a toolkit made to remove boilerplate. 22 Outside React, the mainstream has moved to tracked reads. Angular, Vue, Svelte and Solid build on signals or something equivalent, Preact offers them, and Svelte’s team put it this way: “we’ve come to the realisation that Knockout was right all along.” 23 Inside React, Jotai and MobX bring tracking in as libraries, and Legend-State even offers a “render once” style. 24 Most applications are still on React, and React’s team disagrees, which I come back to below. So the convergence is on the state model, outside one large exception.

items.title: Cruise ship pianist rescued from sea after nine hours in Pacific Ocean
items.summary: Two US fishermen say they spotted the man treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast.
items.content:
A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports.

Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.

"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him.

The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident.

The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas.

"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.

The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from "a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water".

The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said.

Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered.

"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS.

Norton credited the man's survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures.

"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said, which equates to about 24C.

The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average.

In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time.

"To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

items.title: RIP, Harvest
items.summary: Article URL: https://aphyr.com/posts/427-rip-harvest Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50420035 Points: 342 # Comments: 101
items.content:
I’ve been a self-employed contractor for about a decade now, and I’m bummed about Harvest .

Harvest was a time-tracking and invoicing service. You’d track how many hours or weeks you spent on a project, put together an invoice, email it to the client, and close it out when they paid. There was a little Stripe integration for accepting credit and ACH payments on the invoice web view. A historical chart of total billed/paid amounts over time, and a table of invoices. Harvest was exactly what you want from small-business software: it solved a well-defined problem with a reliable, simple interface, and did so at a reasonable monthly price. They managed to avoid scope creep and never tried to become an accounting platform, or a blockchain for washing machines. 1 I loved Harvest and raved about it to every self-employed person I met.

Back in 2025 Harvest got bought out by Bending Spoons , the company that gutted Vimeo . I was worried they might ruin it, but was busy with other things and didn’t have time to look for new invoicing software.

Long story short, they raised my price from $13.32 to $133.98 per month by moving everyone to a new “enterprise” plan and “unlimited” usage billing model, which is, as far as I can tell, exactly what I had before. There’s also a “flex” plan which costs $12.65 per month… but that plan now skims an additional 2% on top of the usual ~3% card transaction fees. To be clear, that 3% pays for the whole credit card network, plus all the people working at Stripe and Mastercard, plus the financial risk of chargebacks and fraud, etc. Harvest isn’t doing any of that work. I don’t know about you, but I don’t think I need to spend 2% of my gross revenue to send a couple PDFs a month and wrap a Stripe web form.

I wrote to Harvest about this, and discovered that they don’t read customer emails any more. Instead they have a Large Language Model repeatedly vomit thousands of words at you. I’m no stranger to enshittification, but man, I did not anticipate the speed at which Bending Spoons would drive a perfectly good company into the ground.

Time to find a new invoicing service, I guess. Maybe bookkeeping too—Intuit’s Quickbooks Online seems to have completely jumped the shark. Any of y’all freelancers have a system you like?

items.title: Unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world
items.summary: Article URL: https://shubs.io/unlocking-any-car-from-x-brand-in-most-of-the-world/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50419215 Points: 332 # Comments: 126
items.content:
I've always had a soft spot for this particular car brand. Our family has owned a few of them over the years, and they've served us incredibly well. In 2023, I bought a new four wheel drive/SUV from them, and it was the first time I had access to their connected car platform.

Having looked at platforms like this before ( previous works ), I was sceptical about how secure they really were. I suspected there was something there, but life kept getting in the way of actually looking. This July, I collaborated with Sam Curry to take a look at the security of a major automaker's connected car systems. Throughout this post, I'll refer to them simply as "the automaker".

When you typically think of car hacking, it's often easy to jump into the hardware side of things, but my background sits pretty squarely in compromising internet-facing web applications and infrastructure. Regardless of all the hardware bits and bobs, it all connects back to some service that, by design, has to be reachable from the internet.

The journey started with a simple question: what infrastructure does the app talk to when I remotely unlock my car? To work this out, I downloaded the APK and decompiled it, eventually reconstructing the API requests that were being made.

Going through the code, the primary point of contact seemed to be assets under *.redacted-telematics.com.au :

Almost every part of the consumer application called back to redacted-telematics.com.au . What else existed under this domain?

Running connected car infrastructure can be quite complex, and managing it requires a mix of admin tools, staging, dev, and QA environments, to make sure that customers get a clean experience. Whether all of that should be sitting on the public internet, available to anyone willing to do some basic reconnaissance, is a different story.

One asset caught my attention more than the others. admintool.redacted-telematics.com.au returned a page titled TEST HARNESS. Who can resist a subdomain with admintool in it?

Visiting this subdomain presented a very plain and grey login screen, which didn't exactly ooze quality, given it presented a logout button before we'd logged in.

I love that most single-page applications ship their entire JavaScript bundle even when all they need to render is a login page. Sure, some more modern frameworks split out JavaScript files so that they only serve what is necessary, but in this case, we could comb through the large JavaScript bundle to understand what this "admin tool" actually let you do.

Turns out this admin tool let you do quite a lot. It had a rich API that let the automaker's employees interact with customer accounts and production vehicles with very few restrictions. Reconstructing the requests, we found that a lot of these APIs needed no authentication beyond the hardcoded API keys sitting in the JavaScript bundle.

For example, we could look up user accounts by email address:

But that's just not good enough. If we want to unlock any of their cars from just knowing the number plate, we're going to need to do better than that.

In Australia, a number plate gets you the VIN (vehicle identification number) fairly easily through state-based registration lookup sites.

This isn't really a security flaw. There are plenty of legitimate reasons to want a VIN, like checking a car's true repair and insurance history before buying second-hand. If we could go from VIN to a subscriber or email, we'd complete the chain.

With the subscriber GUID, you could pull the full account details (including the user's email via the /v1/account endpoint) like so:

Well, I guess we have the first part of our chain sorted. Plate -> VIN -> Subscriber GUID -> User Account PII (email) registered on the automaker's identity platform (ForgeRock OpenIDM).

Now, how do we send commands to any car we want? Surely this admin tool would let us do that? Unfortunately, no. It let us provision features to a car, add ourselves to a user's account as a secondary user, and even generate remote access codes. But for all that functionality, none of it actually got us remote control of a vehicle.

Sam and I then spent two weeks digging into how the automaker manages their central identity system: the software they use, the way commands are issued, and how consumers authenticate.

When a user goes through the authentication flow for the automaker's mobile app, requests are made to login.redacted-identity.com.au , and after going through an MFA flow, a consumer auth token is finally issued. This auth token is then used for subsequent requests to api.redacted-telematics.com.au (both REST APIs and GraphQL). Once you have that auth token, it's pretty much game over. You can control a user's car (remote unlock/lock, horns, engine, etc).

So if we could mint a token for any user, we'd finally be able to control anyone's connected car. This is the angle we went for.

The automaker is a heavy user of ForgeRock's identity software (OpenAM/OpenIDM). This is the cornerstone of their authentication mechanisms. Pulling the subdomains for *.redacted-identity.com.au , we quickly found their OpenIDM instance at openidm.redacted-identity.com.au . This is the system that manages every identity registered on the automaker's connected car platform.

This all clicked together when we were combing through the JavaScript files under *.redacted-telematics.com.au and we came across an absolutely cursed vendor JavaScript bundle that embedded admin credentials for OpenIDM 😱:

Even though these admin credentials were meant to be for their staging environment, given the hygiene we'd seen so far, we were pretty sure they'd work in production too.

Looking closer at OpenIDM, we couldn't tell whether the automaker knew how fragile it was. One thing was obvious though: they'd invested heavily in WAF rules to block access to the sensitive APIs that ForgeRock typically lets you call via /openidm/* .

Even with the origin IP, any request to /openidm/ came straight back as an Nginx WAF block. Someone had put real effort into hardening these assets (despite them being externally accessible).

Fair enough, and we respect the hardening. But that much WAF investment usually means bandaids over something known to be bad. They probably understood how bad it was to have this asset exposed at all, and some business case kept it there anyway.

I'm not sure a WAF rule has ever stopped us when we're motivated enough, so we invested days into finding a way out of these protections, using our trusty path traversal tricks. How hard could it be?

Validating the admin credentials we found inside the JavaScript bundle was not that tough. The Australian OpenIDM instance had a few paths whitelisted like /XUI/ and /UI/ , and path traversal characters were not blocked, so something as simple as /XUI/..%2fopenidm/endpoint seemed to at least partially work:

But it can never be as simple as that, right? The path traversal still didn't get us to the endpoints under /openidm/ , thanks to quirks in how OpenIDM handles routing. Every endpoint would error out like so:

In OpenIDM's world, there were no servlets (or resources) registered against paths that included the path traversal within them. So it would just error out, even though it issued us an admin JWT.

We were incredibly annoyed by this. A simple quirk in routing mechanisms (probably not even designed as a security consideration) was blocking the full attack chain from working. We sat frustrated for a few days, and we thought that the path traversal angle just wasn't going to work. We did find a few other endpoints (user upload, for example) that looked like they might work, but we hit another quirk, a servlet path check, that prevented us from using them meaningfully.

All of this made us ask a different question: why expose these OpenIDM instances externally at all? Surely there had to be some legitimate use case for these assets to be exposed on the internet? We went back to the different JavaScript bundles we had collected from their assets and searched them for communications to OpenIDM. We turned to the decompiled Android application and found the following:

These were clearly endpoints within their OpenIDM asset that were contactable from the Android app. So, maybe these were accessible without the WAF getting in the way?

What other custom endpoints existed? With some very light brute forcing and guessing, we quickly found a getUser endpoint. Guessing at parameters, we found it accepted mail , guid , and phone . Combined with our admin credentials, what did this really let us do?

The response came back with the password hash, PIN code hash, mobile push tokens, and PII including mobile numbers and full names. There was no WAF block on this endpoint, so no path traversal was needed and the correct servlet responded.

Don't get me wrong, this was already pretty impactful. But the passwords were hashed with PBKDF2-SHA512, and needing time on a hash cracking rig for every unlock, with no guarantee of success, felt a bit lacklustre.

Back to the drawing board. How could we access the /openidm/managed/user servlet with our path traversal, and still have the path be recognised by OpenIDM? We grabbed the OpenIDM source closest to the version we were testing against and let GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra spend a good six hours on it.

items.title: I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists
items.summary: Article URL: https://matteoraso.github.io/im-not-convinced-the-ai-bubble-exists.html#im-not-convinced-the-ai-bubble-exists Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50418975 Points: 263 # Comments: 425
items.content:
The AI bubble is a speculative concept that the AI industry is extremely over-valued. If true, the value of most companies involved in AI (several of whom are worth well over a trillion dollars) will collapse, devastating the entire economy. If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now. I don't think that this is a reasonable assumption, though. Nobody can see the future, but I think that there's a pretty realistic chance that the meteoritic growth of AI companies in the past few years is justified, and that they have even more room for growth.

To say that AI companies are spending an absurd amount of money is an understatement. The debt and spending commitments for AI companies are handled through complex vehicles that make it difficult to tell exactly how much their expenses actually are (a serious problem, and one of the most salient points in favour of AI being a bubble), but they've committed to spending at least 3 trillion dollars so far . It's also been estimated that AI companies have already spent 1.9 trillion , bringing the overall expense of the AI industry to around 5 trillion dollars. This is unprecedented levels of investment, and AI just can't be profitable if this level of spending is maintained. However, there's no reason for why this level of spending has to be maintained in the first place. The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.

Outside of these expenses, AI doesn't cost that much to run. We don't have the full numbers for the entire industry here, but Anthropic's S-1 filing says that they make $2.08 for every $1 of compute. In other words, once you ignore the cost of building infrastructure, AI is very profitable. Crucially, the S-1 filing indicates that Anthropic has started to make more than their compute and infrastructure investments combined, which cuts against the idea that the cost of building data centres is inherently unsustainable. In a pinch, AI companies can also cut costs by no longer allowing people to use their products for free and temporarily suspending expensive AI research. This can be implemented instantly, whereas other kinds of expenses like leases and spending commitments are a lot harder to cut.

The only serious long-term expenses to contend with here is the massive amount of debt that's been taken out to pay for these data centres in the first place. Like I said before, it's hard to really figure out these commitments because of the complex way that they're issued, but we can do some back of the envelope math. If the AI industry has to pay off 5 trillion dollars over the course of 20 years, that's 250 billion dollars a year. For context, Alphabet (parent company of Google and Youtube) reported earning almost 162 billion dollars of revenue just in 2019. Adjusted for inflation, that's an even more impressive 213 billion dollars. Because this is very rough math, the total needed revenue might come in to well over 250 billion dollars a year, but the point stands. Even though this is an enormous expense, paying it off isn't unthinkable with the data we have so far. Some of the debt is in convertible notes as well, which can be repaid through shares instead of cash. In the first 6 months of 2026, Anthropic has recorded 72 billion dollars of loss in the form of shares that are due to lenders. The cost is only so high because the valuation has skyrocketed to an estimated 1 trillion dollars, which means that Anthropic has more than enough equity to make lenders whole.

In their S-1 filing, Anthropic records their revenue going from 41 million in 2023, 386 million in 2024, 4.585 billion in 2025, and 16.3 billion in the first 6 months of 2026. That's an insane increase in revenue, and it's safe to assume that other major AI companies like OpenAI are also seeing similar increases as well. At some point, the rate of increase has to level off, but that doesn't have to happen anytime soon. When I look at the current capacity of AI, it really feels like there's so much potential for frontier models to be used that just aren't being applied yet. Most (or maybe even all) programmers and mathematicians are worse at their respective field than an AI swarm equipped with a good harness, and a good deal more expensive as well. AI can't replace lawyers and doctors, but they can automate their paperwork and free up time for them to do other things. Outside of generative AI, self-driving cars are becoming a reality, with some evidence to suggest that they're even better than human drivers. AI adoption takes time, but there's no reason to think that AI usage isn't going to massively skyrocket, even if AI doesn't get any better than it is today (and it certainly will get better). In other words, there's massive unmet demand for AI companies to profit from.

There's a weird contradiction you see from AI skeptics where they're afraid of how AI will change the world, but also seem convinced that AI will only ever produce slop that nobody would ever pay money for. You can't really have it both ways here. It's completely valid to be afraid of AI taking your job, but money is going to change hands when that happens. I don't know exactly what the future will look like or how long it'll take for mass AI adoption to really happen, but when I imagine how AI will change the world, it's hard for me to see AI consumption not being 10x what it is now.

In 2023, a memo from Google called "We Have No Moat, And Neither Does OpenAI" was leaked, which outlined how the open source community was keeping pace with AI labs. More broadly, the memo rejected the idea that any company can really have a durable advantage when it comes to AI development. It would certainly be profitable if they could, but there's already so much information and research out there that nobody can ever hope for their frontier models to stay on the frontier for long. That means that there will never be a point where a company wins the AI wars, just nonstop fighting as each company in the industry tries to one-up the others. You know what other company didn't have a moat and found itself in a war to sell a product that its competitors could easily copy? Popeyes during the chicken sandwich war . I know that sounds goofy, but from a business perspective, it's remarkably similar. None of the restaurants involved in the chicken sandwich war had an enduring competitive advantage over any of the others, and all of them had to deal with potential customers choosing to just cookat home instead, but it was still highly profitable for everybody involved. Simply saying that a company doesn't have a moat isn't enough to say that the company can't make money.

In theory, an AI company has to be worried about their users switching over to a competitor or using an open source model instead. In practice, this isn't a major concern. For starters, the average person isn't going to use a locally hosted model, ever. I know that it's a common hobby in tech circles, but normal users don't want to have to deal with the hassle or expense of setting up something that's going to perform at most the exact same as ChatGPT. That means that in principle, there's only going to be a few models that the vast majority of people will ever use. People can theoretically switch from model to model, but people tend to settle in with a product and develop brand loyalty. For example, I pretty much only use ChatGPT, not because I have any really reason to, but because it was the first LLM that I ever used. This partially offsets the risk of losing customers to a different product. Another way that companies can make money without having a moat is through institutional lock-in. Once a large corporation has integrated a particular AI into their day to day operation, transitioning away isn't costless. They may even have contracts agreeing to buy a certain amount of tokens, which binds them to keep using the AI instead of transitioning.

A potential way for a bubble to pop is for the companies involved to run out of capital to spend while they grow, causing them to fail. With the enormous amount of churn and debt that AI companies have, this is a serious risk to consider. Even so, I think that it's premature to worry about these companies failing to raise capital when most of them haven't even had an IPO yet. When SpaceX (which is partially an AI company, despite the name) went public, they raised more than 80 billion dollars . Besides that, many AI companies haven't issued public debt yet, which is a major way to get loans if private lenders decide that they don't want to put more of their capital into AI. The ones that have issued public debt, like Alphabet and Meta, have excellent bond ratings. If they need more capital, they won't struggle to find people to give them a loan.

items.title: Surgeon having lunch near Krakow shooting undoubtedly saved officer's life, colleague says
items.summary: Further details have emerged about two police officers hailed for preventing a Polish gunman from killing more.
items.content:
One of two surgeons who treated victims on the streets in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.

The pair were eating near the city's Main Market Square on Saturday when a gunman began firing at random, killing six people and injuring 15.

The doctors raced to treat both the attacker and two officers shot while subduing the perpetrator.

On Sunday, the officers - both hailed as "true heroes" by the prime minister for preventing further deaths - emerged from comas.

Prosecutors launched a terror investigation after ministers previously said the 24-year-old Polish attacker - who remains in a critical condition - was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies".

A British national and Austrian woman were among those killed alongside four Poles.

Professor Michal Pędziwiatr was having lunch with a colleague, named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, and their families in central Krakow when they heard gunshots.

Pędziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible.

"We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."

He said his colleague used his hand to stem the bleeding from the most injured policeman, allowing them to wait for an ambulance which transferred the officer to hospital.

Pędziwiatr said they came to learn that one of those they treated was the apparent attacker.

"As a doctor... it doesn't matter to me if it's a victim or a suspect," he said.

"It's not our task to decide what to do with this guy... for us, it was another heavily injured victim, that's all."

According to local media, Wierdak is a renowned surgeon in Krakow. The University Hospital in Krakow states Pędziwiatr is head of General, Oncological, Metabolic and Emergency Surgery.

The police officers have been identified as senior constables Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański.

When his house was searched after the attack in central Krakow, the bodies of his parents and sister were found.

The National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland launched an investigation into the attack with a unit specialising in "terrorist offences" taking the lead.

Separately, reports emerged that six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers also assisted in the aftermath of the shooting.

James McConnell, an officer, told RTE News the group were on a city break and were close to the main square , external when the shooting happened.

The volunteers who are trained to provide medical care immediately sought to help injured people, providing "CPR and haemorrhage control".

Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded.

Ruby Catherine Warren, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".

Not knowing where the gunman was - or if there was more than one - they "just kept sprinting", eventually finding a hotel to hide inside.

Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover".

"I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away," he said.

The suspect wore full military tactical gear during the attack and was described as having a military-grade weapon - but the government said he was not a member of the Polish armed forces.

Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said "everything suggests" the suspect was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held ultra-nationalist views.

The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) on Saturday in the historic centre of Krakow.

Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.

The glass fronts of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.

The mayor of Krakow said he had submitted an urgent request for the two officers injured while stopping the attacker to be awarded titles of honorary citizens of the city.

Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.

items.title: Guerra Ucraina - Russia, le news di oggi. Rubio: “Progressi sulla sicurezza dopo la fine del conflitto”
items.summary: Oggi partono le prime esercitazioni militari della Forza multinazionale per l'Ucraina (Man-u), il "braccio militare" dei Volenterosi in vista del dopoguerra
items.content:
“Sono stati compiuti progressi su come potrebbe configurarsi "l'infrastruttura di sicurezza" dell'Ucraina e dell'Europa dopo la guerra e con la Russia, e ulteriori passi in avanti potrebbero verificarsi nei colloqui dei prossimi giorni a Abu Dhabi”. Lo ha detto il segretario di Stato Marco Rubio prima di partire per Parigi, dove oggi parteciperà al G7 dei ministri degli Esteri.

Oggi partono le prime esercitazioni militari della Forza multinazionale per l'Ucraina (Man-u), il "braccio militare" dei Volenterosi in vista del dopoguerra. Si terranno principalmente in Polonia, ma anche in Turchia e Francia. In campo, sino al 22 novembre, 2.800 soldati.

Cremlino: “Ad Abu Dhabi è un trilaterale, gli europei non partecipano”

Zelensky: “Con il pretesto dell’operazione umanitaria, Mosca ha dispiegato ulteriori forze a Oleshky”

Zelensky sente von der Leyen: “Coordinate le posizioni in vista del vertice di Abu Dhabi”

Von der Leyen conferma: “L’Ue presente ai colloqui di Abu Dhabi”

Cremlino: “Ad Abu Dhabi è un trilaterale, gli europei non partecipano”

Il Cremlino ha precisato che il format del vertice di Abu Dhabi è un trilaterale con Usa, Russia e Ucraina, e che dunque gli europei, pur presenti, non partecipano al summit.

Zelensky: “Con il pretesto dell’operazione umanitaria, Mosca ha dispiegato ulteriori forze a Oleshky”

Le truppe russe, con la scusa di un'operazione umanitaria, hanno dispiegato ulteriori forze a Oleshky , città temporaneamente occupata, e nella comunità circostante. Lo ha scritto sui social il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky, dopo aver incontrato i capi delle amministrazioni regionali. "Purtroppo, con la scusa di un'operazione umanitaria a Oleshky, l'esercito russo ha effettuato un importante cambio di personale e mezzi sulla riva sinistra. Ulteriori forze di occupazione sono state dispiegate a Oleshky e nella comunità circostante. Il comando delle Forze Armate ucraine deve presentare proposte per una maggiore protezione della vita a Kherson dal terrore russo", ha osservato il capo dello Stato.

Zelensky sente von der Leyen: “Coordinate le posizioni in vista del vertice di Abu Dhabi”

Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky ha affermato di aver parlato con la presidente della Commissione europea Ursula von der Leyen. "Abbiamo coordinato le nostre posizioni in vista dell'incontro ad Abu Dhabi. Stiamo facendo tutto il possibile affinché il formato trilaterale porti a risultati concreti", ha scritto il leader su X. Domani e mercoledì sono in programma gli incontri trilaterali tra gli emissari di Kiev, Washington e Mosca ad Abu Dhabi. Von der Leyen ha affermato che anche l'Ue parteciperà ai colloqui.

I spoke with President of the European Commission Ursula @vonderLeyen. Right now, many of our cities and communities are facing a very difficult situation with power, water, and heating supplies due to Russian strikes. The situation is most difficult in Kyiv, the Dnipro, Sumy, and Donetsk regions, and Kherson. I told Ursula about the challenges, and we agreed that the European Union would activate a special emergency mechanism. This will make it possible to quickly provide Ukraine with funding for what is needed most right now. Our teams are already working on this. We discussed additional energy and humanitarian assistance to prepare for winter, as well as issues related to European integration. Last week, the European Commission published its annual EU Enlargement Package, which gave a positive assessment of Ukraine’s progress. It is important to open all the clusters and begin closing the chapters. Of course, we also discussed diplomacy. In recent days, talks were held in Brussels, where our teams did a good job working on a recovery plan and security guarantees from Europe. Ursula and I also coordinated our positions regarding the meeting in Abu Dhabi. We are doing everything to ensure that the trilateral format delivers results. Thank you, Ursula!

La Russia ha registrato la morte di circa 400mila suoi cittadini impegnati nei combattimenti in Ucraina dall'inizio dell'invasione su vasta scala, quasi cinque anni fa. Lo riferisce Bloomberg , citando dati riservati dell'agenzia statistica russa Rosstat. Le informazioni provengono da oltre 11 milioni di certificati di morte, corredati da dettagli quali residenza, età e luogo del decesso. I dati sono stati ottenuti dal gruppo bielorusso vicino all'opposizione Cyber Partisans e dal gruppo di hacker ucraino Silent Crow, che li hanno successivamente condivisi con Bloomberg News e un ristretto numero di altre testate.

Governatore di Leningrado: “Una donna uccisa dai rottami di un drone”

Una donna è morta in un attacco di droni ucraini nella regione di Leningrado , ha riferito il governatore, Aleksandr Drozdenko. "Nella città di Vsevolozhsk, una donna che viveva in un appartamento all'ultimo piano è rimasta uccisa quando i detriti di un drone sono caduti sul tetto dell'edificio. Inoltre, nel distretto di Kirishi, un drone ha colpito lo stabilimento petrolchimico Kinef, provocando un incendio, riferisce l'emittente Vesti. Nella medesima città sono stati danneggiati gli impianti di riscaldamento.

Von der Leyen conferma: “L’Ue presente ai colloqui di Abu Dhabi”

"L'Ue sarà presente insieme ai nostri partner ai colloqui di Abu Dhabi di questa settimana". Lo ha annunciato la presidente della Commissione europea, Ursula von der Leyen, in un messaggio sui social, riferendo di una telefonata avuta con il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky alla vigilia della sua visita nella regione del Mar Nero. "Abbiamo discusso degli sforzi di pace in corso e dei colloqui di Abu Dhabi di questa settimana, ai quali l'Ue sarà presente insieme ai nostri partner", ha scritto von der Leyen. "Oggi inizio una visita nella regione del Mar Nero", ha ricordato.

Today, I begin a visit to the Black Sea region, where security threats are escalating, attacks are increasing, and innocent lives have been lost. In Romania and Bulgaria, I will meet with leaders to discuss the situation on the ground and how Europe can strengthen its response. Ahead of the visit, I had a good call with President @ZelenskyyUA Freedom of navigation in the Black Sea must be restored and preserved. I reiterated my support for his call for a ceasefire covering food and energy infrastructure. We also discussed ongoing peace efforts and the talks in Abu Dhabi this week, where the EU will be present alongside our partners. I look forward to meeting President Zelenskyy in Dublin later this week and discussing the next steps towards peace with fellow leaders.

Mosca: “L'Ucraina e gli alleati europei si preparano a proseguire la guerra”

Kiev e i suoi alleati europei si stanno preparando a continuare la guerra, ha dichiarato il Segretario del Consiglio di Sicurezza russo, Serghei Shoigu. "Sembra che l'Ucraina e i suoi alleati europei si stiano preparando alla guerra, alla sua continuazione, e non alla pace", ha affermato Shoigu, citato da Tass .

Droni ucraini colpiscono una raffineria di petrolio a 800 chilometri dal confine

Nella notte, dei droni ucraini hanno colpito la seconda raffineria di petrolio più grande della Russia, situata a Kirisi, nell'oblast di Leningrado; a riferirlo sono diversi canali di monitoraggio ucraini citati da Ukrainska Pravda . L'attacco ha provocato forti esplosioni nell'impianto petrolifero, che si trova a circa 800 chilometri a nord dell'Ucraina, secondo quanto riportato dai canali di monitoraggio Exilenova+ e Supernova+. Il sistema Firms (Fire Information for Resource Management System) della Nasa, che utilizza dati satellitari per rilevare anomalie termiche e incendi, ha individuato diversi punti di calore presso l'impianto. Aleksandr Drozdenko, governatore dell'oblast di Leningrado, ha dichiarato che, durante l'attacco, sono stati abbattuti complessivamente 113 droni ucraini sopra la regione.

I sistemi di difesa aerea della russia. Hanno intercettato e distrutto 430 droni ucraini nei cieli di diverse regioni russe durante la notte: lo ha riferito a mosca il ministero della difesa. Le comunicazioni sono state rilanciate dall'agenzia di stampa tass. "Nel corso della notte", ha riferito il ministero, "le forze di difesa aerea hanno intercettato e distrutto 430 velivoli senza pilota ucraini ad ala fissa sui territori delle regioni di belgorod, brjansk, voronezh, kaluga, kursk, leningrado, lipetsk, mosca, oriol, pskov, smolensk, tambov, tver e tula, oltre che sulla repubblica di crimea".

"Credo che riusciremo a concludere, credo che accadrà; l'Ucraina finirà per avere una configurazione un po' diversa". Lo ha dichiarato il presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump in un'intervista rilasciata al programma '60 Minutes', esprimendo le sue aspettative riguardo ai negoziati di pace tra Russia e Ucraina. Riferendosi ai imminenti negoziati di pace trilaterali tra Stati Uniti, Ucraina e Russia, previsti ad Abu Dhabi per il 10 e l'11 novembre, Trump ha affermato di ritenere che "siamo molto vicini a raggiungere un accordo". "È in corso un incontro molto importante", ha detto Trump come riportano i media americani. "Credo che questa guerra finirà, e finirà presto. E l'unico motivo per cui finirà è merito mio".

items.title: KetchUp – Open-source SketchUp alternative built with Rust and WebGPU
items.summary: Article URL: https://ketchup3d.github.io/app/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50418176 Points: 474 # Comments: 131
items.content:
BenchUp is a free, open-source 3D modeling app for woodworking and furniture design. Plan a shelf, table, cabinet, or workbench with exact measurements before you build. Use it on Windows, macOS, Linux, or right in your desktop browser.

Free & open source. No account needed. Made for a desktop browser and a mouse.

Start with a simple shape. Keep the tools you need close, and your model at the center.

Sketch lines, rectangles, circles, and freehand outlines. Turn faces into forms with Push/Pull, then move, scale, offset, and paint.

Snap to geometry and axes, type exact lengths, and add dimensions. Organize the bigger picture with groups, components, and tags.

Autosave locally and download portable .ketchup projects. Import SketchUp geometry or export an OBJ to take your model further.

For woodworkers, furniture makers, and DIY builders who want to explore a project in 3D.

Draw board outlines with rectangles and lines, then use Push/Pull to give them thickness. Move and copy geometry to explore shelves, tables, cabinets, workbenches, and other furniture.

Enter exact lengths, snap to geometry and axes, and use Tape Measure and Dimensions to inspect your design. Orbit around the assembly to review proportions before taking it to the workshop.

Use groups, reusable components, and tags to organize parts. Save a portable .ketchup project locally, import SketchUp geometry, or export OBJ geometry for another 3D workflow.

Start with the browser editor or download the desktop app . Read the user guide for modeling instructions and supported workflows.

The editor opens with a clean slate. Here’s a good place to start.

Click one corner, then the opposite corner to create your first face.

Choose Push/Pull, click the face, move your mouse, and click to finish.

Choose Orbit and drag to look around. Scroll to zoom; press F to fit your model.

A desktop browser with hardware acceleration and WebGPU or WebGL2 support. Use a mouse and keyboard for modeling. You can also run BenchUp as a native Windows, macOS, or Linux app.

Your model is autosaved in this browser on this device. Use File → Save to download a .ketchup project you can keep or open again. Clearing browser data can remove autosaved work, so download projects you want to keep. There’s no cloud storage or account to set up.

Use File → Import/Export to import SketchUp (.skp) geometry or export Wavefront OBJ (.obj). Imports run locally. SketchUp textures, scenes, and some model features aren’t supported; OBJ export includes geometry without materials.

Yes. BenchUp is open source under the MIT license and written in Rust. Explore the code, read the full guide, or contribute on GitHub.

I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.

To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.

To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.

Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.

My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.

items.title: Aramco Tower hit in heart of Saudi capital as Houthis launch fresh strikes
items.summary: Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows damage to the building in the capital's central financial district.
items.content:
The Aramco Tower, a skyscraper in the Saudi Arabian capital's central financial district, had been hit by an air attack.

A statement issued via the Houthi-controlled Saba news agency confirmed the group had targeted Riyadh's business zone on Saturday, without mentioning the Aramco Tower by name.

The Saudi energy ministry said the tower had suffered only "minor damage" and no one had been killed or injured.

Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows more extensive damage to the building, with at least one floor appearing to have been badly hit by a missile or drone strike.

Windows on more than one level appear to have been shattered by the strike.

The Houthis also said Riyadh's airport and Aramco oil storage facilities were targeted in separate strikes. Saudi Arabia said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed several missiles.

The strikes were the latest claimed by the Yemen-based armed group against targets deep inside Saudi Arabia, which the Gulf power has struggled to contain in recent months.

It came a day after the Houthis accused a Saudi-led coalition of killing at least 33 people , including women and children, in an air strike on Yemen.

Footage broadcast by Houthi-run television channel Al Masirah showed rescuers pulling bodies from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.

Saba said 39 people had been injured in the strike. Saudi Arabia has not commented.

A Saudi-led coalition has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government, which has lost control of a large swathe of the country to the rebel group.

Although the conflict had largely been dormant in recent years, fighting has intensified following the outbreak of the Iran war.

An informal ceasefire unravelled in July after the Tehran-backed Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport Saudi Arabia said had been to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing there.

Major fighting has since resumed between Houthi forces and troops aligned with Yemen's Saudi-backed government.

The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.

items.title: Manovra alla Camera, il governo vuole solo piccole modifiche
items.summary: Assedio delle categorie. Cgil lancia allarme taglio pensioni. Atteso il dl bollette in Cdm
items.content:
Tutto ancora tace. Alla vigilia dell'avvio dell'esame della manovra alla Camera, il ministro dell'Economia Giancarlo Giorgetti, non dice una parola sulla legge di bilancio, intervenendo al congresso provinciale della Lega di Varese.

Domani a parlare saranno le tante realtà audite dalla commissione Bilancio, oltre 30 in un giorno, dagli studenti al terzo settore, dalle assicurazioni alle costruzioni e alla proprietà immobiliare, fino alla Corte dei conti. Ognuna con le sue richieste di modifiche e correzioni. Per presentare gli emendamenti c'è tempo fino al 17 novembre. A Parlamento e Governo poi il compito di limare il provvedimento, mantenendo solido l'impianto. I saldi difficilmente potranno cambiare: gli interventi saranno limitati.

Il conto per i pensionati è salato. Lo Spi Cgil stima in 100 miliardi di euro la mancata rivalutazione delle pensioni tra il 2023 e il 2036, subita da meno di 4 milioni di persone. I nuovi tagli si sommano, infatti, a quelli degli anni precedenti. In un arco di tempo più limitato, dal 2023 al 2027, la perdita netta va da 1.818 euro all'anno per chi percepisce pensioni da 2.200 euro al mese lordi fino a 10.510 euro all'anno per le pensioni da 4.300 euro. "Vediamo l'impoverimento anche di chi è in pensione dopo aver lavorato tutta la vita", ha affermato la segretaria generale dello Spi Cgil, Tania Scacchetti.

Scuola e sanità sono tematiche aperte. Il presidente di Noi Moderati, Maurizio Lupi, propone di destinare le risorse risparmiate con i 7mila tagli previsti, tra docenti e personale Ata, per pagare di più gli insegnanti e migliorare la qualità dell'istruzione.

Mentre dall'opposizione, Elly Schlein denuncia il rischio che la sanità venga smantellata, "lo stanno dicendo anche le regioni di destra": il governo ha stanziato 2 miliardi quando il ministro ne chiedeva 5,5. Il Pd si batterà anche per evitare la stretta sulle fondazioni bancarie, nella convinzione che porti un gettito modesto ma un danno sociale certo.

Emerge poi il caso delle tasse "invisibili", prelievi su tabacchi, giochi e bollette che hanno un valore di almeno 5 miliardi, secondo quanto calcolato dal Sole24ore. In particolare la manovra prevede un aumento degli oneri di sistema nelle bollette per 2,6 miliardi di euro nel biennio 2029-2030. Il prelievo aggiuntivo potrebbe raggiungere 100 euro a utenza.

"I nostri parlamentari sono pronti a migliorare il testo", assicura intanto Matteo Salvini nella newsletter "La settimana leghista" dove ribadisce le priorità: pensioni, sicurezza, opportunità per i giovani, sostegno alle famiglie e alla scuola. "Ci aspettano settimane decisive", osserva.

Domani è atteso anche in Consiglio dei ministri - dopo due rinvii - il decreto bollette bis, che mira a ridurre le tariffe elettriche mettendo un tetto al prezzo del gas. L'ultimo slittamento, giovedì scorso, sarebbe stato dovuto ai rilievi della Ragioneria dello Stato su una norma secondaria. Non sono previste modifiche sostanziali al cuore del decreto, la misura che prevede un tetto al prezzo del gas per la produzione elettrica a circa 59 euro al megawattora, sul modello del 'tope' iberico. Per le famiglie, il think tank sul clima Ecco, prevede un risparmio di 1,4 euro al mese, a fronte di rincari delle bollette da febbraio a oggi di più di 30 euro al mese.

Sul fronte dei carburanti, intanto, è quiete apparente. Nel primo giorno dopo la scadenza del taglio delle accise, i prezzi medi restano fermi a 2,000 euro al litro per la benzina e 2,223 euro per il diesel sulla rete stradale, secondo i dati dell'Osservatorio del ministero delle Imprese, che attribuisce il merito al price cap posto da molte compagnie. Aiuta anche il recente andamento delle quotazioni del petrolio e il fatto che la domenica molti impianti siano chiusi. Non sono esclusi rincari nei prossimi giorni.

items.title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
items.summary: Several carriages derailed after two trains travelling in the same direction crashed outside the city of Giza.
items.content:
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.

The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.

Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.

Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".

The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.

The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.

Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.

The Egyptian Red Crescent said it was providing aid and psychological support to victims and their families at the scene.

The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.

The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.

Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.

Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains. The railway authority has not said how long it expects this to take.

The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.

In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.

There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.

Foreign leaders and dignitaries have shared condolences and support for the victims.

Saudi Arabia's ministry of foreign affairs expressed "solidarity" with Egypt and wished those hurt a speedy recovery.

Turkey's ambassador to Egypt wrote on X that he extended "heartfelt condolences and sincere sympathy" to the victims, their families, and the Egyptian people.

items.title: The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford
items.summary: Article URL: https://ftrain.com/aboard-the-web-is-more-than-enough Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50416456 Points: 136 # Comments: 82
items.content:
Last week was fun. We launched tinylittleoffice.com —you heard it here first!—and it turned out that lots of folks were in the market for an “office suite that stores data in the URL.”

So many people visited that the server went down (well, I maxxed out the CloudFlare free plan), and ultimately, after I put in my credit card, a couple hundred thousand people came by to check it out. People on Hacker News insisted it was a pointless waste of time, and folks on GitHub started asking for features and fixes, all of which we’re considering, and some of which we’re doing. The Register wrote an article about it , and it also made it, for a little while, to the top ten of Product Hunt .

So all good; we will continue to support and enhance it, bit by bit, while we also do stable software development work for our customers and clients. But I did want to pause for a second and point out something that surprised me about the process. It’s this:

The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for building applications.

I know that is obvious and is the sort of thing I could have said any time in the last 20 years. But now there’s an addendum to the statement:

The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for applications, and the cost of accessing that power is going down seemingly every day.

I put maybe twice as much effort into building a web-based office suite as I might normally put into writing a long newsletter post. I’m not telling you this because I am a very special boy. I’m telling you because if you want to, you can learn to do it, too.

Fast, cheap, good, right? But even after I had to put in my credit card, CloudFlare hosting costs…$0. Partly because I optimize for cheapness, but partly because that’s just how it goes these days. Fast? Dear God, computers are fast, and software development is also fast compared to the past. But as I code web apps, I keep finding new corners of the browser I didn’t know well. Things are just…wild in there.

And on and on. The web is really the greatest distribution platform imaginable right now. It’s inherently multilingual—I released TinyLittleOffice in 21 languages (the most common NYC ones, which is why it has Creole and Yiddish), with lots of infrastructure for accessibility. Plus, of course, JavaScript is a full-featured programming language, and HTML can represent most things a document can do on a computer; if you need something more old-school, PDF.js lets you deal with PDFs in the browser. I think you can even hyphenate text reliably these days, although I refuse to believe it.

I knew these things existed. I’d even programmed with them. But I’d never really looked closely; I just downloaded whatever open-source code would make it easier to build and tried to drag software across the finish line.

My quirky 1990s-vintage office suite might not convince you—it’s weird and small. So take a look at Simon Willison’s new web-based browser 3D game, Battle Drones . He’s hosting it on GitHub. He wrote it himself. He’s not a games builder. It just pops right up in the browser and you play it. It’s multiplayer, and it works offline.

… but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell). I’d love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build!

All the various cool browser technologies have been around for years. But they are each extremely vast. If you get good at Web Audio, you probably don’t have time to get good at Web Crypto and Web Assembly and WebGL.

The reason they were so complex is, basically, because they were built for teams like those at Google, not for individuals. In the past, the web was for people to build web pages—and, yes, in the present, you can still do that, but for more than a decade, the web has been designed for giant companies so they can deliver software securely to billions of people who buy things with credit cards. These huge mega-libraries were dropped into the web browser to enable large teams to build big things, and the little guy was a bit of an afterthought. But now you can make a game in 3D with sound, and it can work just fine on a plane.

This is one of the places where “are we in an AI bubble” gets fuzzy for me, because it’s totally clear all these giant AI companies are huffing AGI paint fumes, but at the same time, if we actually unlocked the economic transformation of, say, 100 times as many people making software for each other, that would blow an enormous crater into the current tech economy. Don’t like the way your giant industrial looms make carpet? Hack your own firmware and make each carpet totally personalized! Turn any Instagram post into a huge floor covering! Suddenly all the carpet companies have to hack their own firmware to compete. What’s that going to be like?

This also destabilizes the app store economy. The high tax of building for app stores seems less worth paying when you can just test an idea in the world from a web server for $0 after a couple weeks. Perhaps Mozilla should take another swing at launching a mobile phone! (Forget I mentioned that.) In any case, what used to be a large industrial process is now a personal one, if you so desire. Web browsers enable incredibly rich app development—and that’s radically easier than it used to be.

It’s a mixed blessing. I’ve been a writer for years, and software development feels more and more like writing to me every passing week. The awkward part of the comparison is, in general, people do not want to pay writers any money at all. As a writer, you get used to it. But for software people, being perpetually devalued is pretty novel. Then again, if you need software to do something—like our clients!—say, to fix a process, organize a database, get more value out of a big piece of industrial equipment, it’s a pretty amazing time, because you can do just about anything. I’m pretty confident we’ll all meet in the middle, but it’ll take a while, and it will be different on the other side.

items.title: How I Fight AI Brain Fry
items.summary: Article URL: https://sergeykuhne.com/blog/fighting-ai-brain-fry Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50416363 Points: 243 # Comments: 170
items.content:
If you work with Claude Code or Codex from the terminal, you know this one.

You start a task. The AI takes time to reply, so you start another one. Then the first one replies, but the reply needs one clarification, one follow up and one side task — and each of them wants its own tab. Then the second tab's reply comes in. You juggle. And all of a sudden you find yourself hopping between 20 threads, trying to keep all those contexts in your brain RAM.

Until you can't. Your brain gets exhausted, your focus smashes, and you don't know anymore what you were doing, where you started, and where you were supposed to finish.

A lot of people are suggesting taking breaks, thinking before typing, limiting scope. I have my own experiment.

I decided this way of working has two major problems: sequencing and context. So I organised my work a bit like a priority queue.

The queue lives in git. Every ticket is a markdown file in the repo, right next to the code it talks about, and the state of the board is a committed snapshot. Nothing important lives in a chat window and nothing lives in my head. If a session dies, the queue is still there.

An agent works that board in cycles. It researches new tickets, builds the ones a human has tagged as safe to build, runs the tests and a browser check, and verifies what is already deployed. For anything touching sensitive code it builds on a branch and asks first. It never deploys to production — that part is mine.

What it cannot do is decide. So everything that needs me lands in one place I call my owner inbox. A script reads the whole board and hands me a prioritised list of exactly the items waiting on my judgement — review this change, answer this question, rule on this tradeoff.

The reading surface is a Claude artifact. One page, rebuilt from git on every cycle, mirroring the whole board plus a review page per ticket. So I don't scroll back through a terminal trying to reconstruct what a change does. I open one link, read what was built and why, and give my verdict. The verdict goes back into git, onto the card. The page is only a viewer — git is the record.

I take one item. I load its context. I make a decision or request an action. And I close it, by putting it back into the queue.

That closing is the whole trick. The ticket doesn't keep hanging in my memory as a thing to remember about. The context closes with it. So when I pick the next item from the queue, I can actually focus. One thing at a time.

It is still exhausting. But I don't feel distracted or lost.

The challenge was, and still is, the tooling around it. Getting the context served up in a digestible manner, so loading a ticket takes a minute and not twenty. And keeping tickets from going into endless loops because they are blocked waiting for a ruling only I can give.

It's a living organism and I keep improving it. But it felt like a huge step forward in my productivity with AI tools, so I thought it was worth sharing.
